title: Integer calendars for fixed-turnover replenishment: a 1/ln 2 guarantee on trees, the price of short cycles and the price of constant gaps
shortTitle: From factor 2 to 1/ln 2 for recurring deliveries
oneLine: Answering Bosman et al.'s 2022 question: rounding each client's clock events, not its period, to whole days gives delivery calendars that never miss a deadline and cost at most 1/ln 2 ≈ 1.44 times the optimum on trees, improving the factor two; constant-gap calendars can reach only about 1.60.
abstract: A depot must revisit every client at least once within that client's turnover time while keeping the long-run average daily routing cost low. Bosman et al. (2022) gave a factor-two approximation on tree networks and asked whether it could be improved. This candidate shows that it can. Every client gets a real-valued clock from one shared power-of-two ladder, the ladder's phase is chosen by a logarithmic averaging argument and an exact breakpoint sweep, and each clock's event times are rounded up to whole days. The calendar meets every deadline and costs at most 1/ln 2 ≈ 1.4427 times the optimum, for any monotone submodular daily cost, of which tree routing is one case; it is computed deterministically in O(n log n) time. It repeats within the longest turnover time, and for such calendars 1/ln 2 is the exact worst-case price; the analysis of the algorithm is tight on trees. Individual gaps may alternate between two consecutive integers. If every client must keep a constant gap, with the gaps dividing one another (the form of Bosman et al.'s output), the best possible worst-case factor lies between 1.6001 and 1.6014, with an explicit four-ladder mixture giving 48/29. The paper also solves the nested two-edge problem exactly, gives divisibility and least-common-multiple criteria for when the frequency lower bound is attained, profiles the cost of longer cycles on the worst-case family, and certifies instances where the optimum exceeds that bound by a factor 1.204. The rounding tools and the constant are classical. AI-assisted, unrefereed candidate; a 2025 master's thesis with a closely matching title could not be obtained, so priority is not claimed; no external peer review, independent reproduction or formal verification is claimed.

keyResults: Integer calendars: rounding the event times of logarithmically phased power-of-two clocks to whole days meets every deadline and costs at most W₁ + (L_f − W₁)/ln 2 ≤ OPT/ln 2 ≈ 1.4427·OPT for any monotone submodular daily cost (Theorem 1); on trees this improves the factor 2 of Bosman et al. (Corollary 1).

Short cycles: the calendar repeats within the longest turnover τ_max, and sup OPT_short/OPT = 1/ln 2 exactly for calendars with that property; the analysis is tight on trees (Theorem 7, eq. (29), Corollary 2).

Constant gaps: if every client keeps a constant gap and the gaps divide one another, the best worst-case factor ρ_H satisfies 1.60010 ≤ ρ_H ≤ 1.60139; mixtures of two and four integer ladders give 12/7 and 48/29 (Theorem 9).

Synchronisation: exact optimum of two nested edges; the frequency bound is attained on a tree iff the edge turnovers divide along every path, and for coverage costs iff lcm{q_A : i ∈ A} ≤ τ_i (Theorems 2, 3, 5).
The frequency lower bound can be loose: certified broom instances have OPT/L_T = 3780/3139 ≈ 1.204.
Worked example: deadlines 2 and 3 on a path; the power-of-two calendar costs 3 per day, the integer calendar 8/3, which is optimal.

narration: From factor two to one over log two: integer calendars for recurring deliveries. An Evidence Press briefing. First, the background. Picture a depot that restocks cash machines or fuel tanks along a branching road network. Each client holds enough stock for a fixed number of days, so it must be visited at least once in every window of that length. Each day a vehicle leaves the depot and returns. Visiting clients on the same road on the same day saves money, but an early visit resets that client's clock, so its next deadline comes sooner too. In 2022, Bosman and colleagues built calendars that cost at most twice the best possible long-run average, and asked whether the factor two could be improved. Now, the main finding. It can. Give every client an internal clock taken from one shared ladder of periods, choose the ladder's position by a logarithmic averaging argument, and round each clock's event times, not its period, up to whole days. No deadline is ever missed, clients sharing a road stay synchronised, and the average cost is at most one over the natural log of two, about one point four four, times the best possible. The calendar repeats within the longest deadline, and for calendars with that property this factor is exactly right. There is a catch: a client's gaps may alternate, for example two days then one. If every client must instead keep a constant gap, with the gaps dividing one another, the best possible factor rises to about one point six. That is still better than two. The limits: the results are mathematical, all test instances are synthetic, review so far is internal and AI-assisted, and a 2025 master's thesis with a similar title could not be obtained, so priority is not claimed. This briefing describes version one point zero candidate, released on the thirty-first of October 2026; the paper and evidence are linked from the release page. This audio uses an AI-generated voice and is not additional evidence.

decisionObject.description: Answers the open question of Bosman et al. (2022, Section 5): the factor-two approximation for min-avg replenishment with fixed turnover times on trees improves to 1/ln 2 with integer-day calendars, exact for calendars repeating within the longest turnover; constant-gap harmonic calendars have best factor between 1.6001 and 1.6014.
decisionObject.scope: Deterministic integer turnover times, long-run average cost, monotone submodular daily costs (trees). No capacity, holding cost, stochastic demand or peak-day objective; general metrics, hardness and general constant-gap policies open.

semanticBridge.description: The feasibility model and optimum are exactly those of Bosman et al. (2022, Section 1); the comparison uses their tree lower bound (Lemma 2). Their outputs are constant-gap; the 1/ln 2 calendars are not, which is stated, and Theorem 9 treats the constant-gap class separately.
